title: GPU Architecture Fundamentals
blurb: Tests the latency and throughput design split between CPUs and GPUs, SIMT and warps, divergence and what modern hardware does about it, SMs and latency hiding, CUDA cores against Tensor Cores, timing GPU work correctly, and reading achieved bandwidth.

refLinks.label: §38.2.4 The Memory Hierarchy, at a Glance

questions.prompt: What is a GPU optimised for, in the chapter's terms?
options: Throughput: lots of uniform work, fast in aggregate
Large caches, so it never has to wait on memory at all
Latency, finishing one thread of branchy work as fast as possible
Branch prediction, so data-dependent code runs at full speed
questions.explanation: A GPU has thousands of simple cores, little branch prediction and no out-of-order execution. It trades single-thread speed for aggregate throughput. Latency, branch prediction and big caches describe the CPU.

questions.prompt: Which workloads does the chapter say GPUs lose at? Select all that apply.
options: Problems too small to fill the GPU and hide memory latency
Branchy control flow that differs per thread
Inherently sequential work where each step needs the last
Large matrix multiplies in deep learning
questions.explanation: Divergent branches, tiny jobs where launch overhead dominates, and sequential dependencies all waste the GPU's parallelism. Matrix multiply is the GPU's home ground, run on Tensor Cores.

questions.prompt: Why does a tiny GPU job, say adding two 1,000-element arrays, often run no faster than on a CPU?
options: Small arrays are always stored in CPU memory, never on the GPU.
GPUs can't add arrays shorter than one warp's worth of elements.
Launch overhead dominates, and there's too little work to fill the GPU.
The GPU must first compile the kernel for every new array length.
questions.explanation: Launch overhead is trivial for a CPU but real for tiny GPU jobs, and a small problem can't supply the parallel work needed to hide memory latency. There is no minimum array length.

questions.prompt: How many threads are in a warp on current NVIDIA hardware?
questions.explanation: A warp is 32 threads that the hardware issues one instruction to at a time. All of them execute that instruction on their own data.

questions.prompt: What is warp divergence?
options: A warp running slower than others because its data is in a slower memory
Two warps on different SMs computing different results for the same input
Warps finishing at different times, so the block has to wait for the very last one to complete
Threads in one warp taking different branches, so the branches may run one after another
questions.explanation: When threads in the same warp split on an if/else, the classic model runs both branches for the whole warp, masking off threads that don't apply. A badly diverged warp could cost the sum of its branches.

questions.prompt: In Listing 38.5, one kernel branches on offs % 2 == 0 and the other on pid % 2 == 0. Why does only the first diverge within a warp?
options: pid is a float and offs is an integer, and only integer conditions diverge.
offs alternates per element. pid is fixed per block.
The second kernel processes fewer elements, so its warps are never full.
The first kernel uses tl.where and the second kernel uses an if statement.
questions.explanation: offs % 2 alternates element by element, splitting each warp about 16/16. pid is one value per program, so every thread in a warp takes the same side. Both kernels use tl.where and the same sizes.

questions.prompt: The divergent kernel took 0.604 ms and the uniform one 0.583 ms. What explains an overhead of about 3.5% rather than about 2x?
options: Volta-era independent thread scheduling, plus cheap branches.
The RTX 5090 has 64-thread warps, so a 16/16 split doesn't count as divergence.
Triton removes all divergence at compile time by rewriting every branch.
The measurement was wrong, since divergence always costs exactly 2x on any NVIDIA hardware.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls this a real finding. Modern scheduling cuts the cost, and the branches here are cheap. A branch with a slow memory access or very different work would diverge more expensively. Warps are still 32 threads.

questions.prompt: What lesson does the chapter draw from the divergence measurement?
options: Divergence no longer matters, so kernels can branch freely per thread.
The classic model overstates the cost now. Measure on the real hardware.
Only Triton kernels avoid divergence costs, so CUDA C++ should be avoided.
Divergence matters more than ever, so all branches should be removed from kernels.
questions.explanation: The chapter says divergence still matters, that its cost depends on what is in each branch, and that measuring beats trusting a rule of thumb. It doesn't say branching is now free.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter call the single most important idea in GPU architecture?
options: Large on-chip caches that remove the need to read global memory
Branch prediction, guessing which way each warp's if statements will go
Latency hiding: switch to a ready warp while others wait on memory
Out-of-order execution, so each thread reorders its own instructions
questions.explanation: An SM keeps many warps in flight and switches to one that is ready whenever another stalls on memory. The CPU tries to avoid stalls with prediction and caches. The GPU hides them with other work.

questions.prompt: Which level of the GPU memory hierarchy is per-SM, fast and managed by the programmer?
options: Global memory (HBM)
Shared memory
L2 cache
Registers
questions.explanation: Shared memory is a slice of fast on-chip memory per SM, tens of KB, that the programmer controls. Registers are per thread. L2 is chip-wide. Global memory is off-chip and largest.

questions.prompt: A colleague picks a GPU because it has the most CUDA cores. What does the chapter say that misses?
options: Nothing. CUDA core count fully decides performance for every workload.
SM count, clocks, bandwidth and Tensor Cores matter too.
Only the price, since every GPU with more cores is faster at the same cost.
Only the power draw, since more cores always means a lower clock speed.
questions.explanation: The chapter names "more CUDA cores means faster" as a common confusion. ML workloads in particular run on Tensor Cores, whose throughput the CUDA core count doesn't capture.

questions.prompt: What does a Tensor Core do?
options: Branch prediction for a warp, so divergent code runs in parallel
One scalar add or multiply per thread, in FP32, FP64 or INT32
A small matrix multiply-accumulate, D = A×B + C, in a few cycles
Copying tensors between host and device memory over PCIe
questions.explanation: Tensor Cores do tile-sized matrix multiply-accumulates at far higher throughput per watt. Scalar arithmetic is what CUDA cores do.

questions.prompt: Why does nearly all of an LLM's compute budget run on Tensor Cores?
options: Tensor Cores are the only units that can run softmax and layer norm.
Tensor Cores have their own memory, so they avoid the bandwidth limit.
CUDA cores are disabled while a model is running in PyTorch.
Its FLOPs are almost all matrix multiplies, such as QKᵀ and the feed-forward layers.
questions.explanation: The 6ND and 2N formulas from Book 2 are dominated by matrix multiplies, which map onto Tensor Cores. Elementwise work runs on CUDA cores, which aren't disabled.

questions.prompt: A GPU's spec sheet gives one TFLOPS figure for ML. What does the chapter say about it?
options: It's a Tensor Core figure, often 10x the CUDA core one.
It is the sum of memory bandwidth and compute, expressed in one unit.
It is the speed of a single SM, to be multiplied by the SM count.
It is the CUDA core number, since Tensor Cores aren't counted in TFLOPS.
questions.explanation: The advertised ML TFLOPS is a Tensor Core figure. An elementwise kernel on CUDA cores will never approach it, and a memory-bound one is limited by bandwidth anyway.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 38.2 run warm-up calls before timing a GPU op?
options: Warm-up calls fill the L2 cache with the answer, so later calls are faster.
The first calls include one-off setup and JIT compiling.
CUDA events can't be created until at least five kernels have run.
The GPU runs slower until its fans reach full speed, which takes several calls.
questions.explanation: Timing the first call is the most common beginner mistake. It includes CUDA context initialisation and kernel compilation, which have nothing to do with steady-state performance.

questions.prompt: What does time.perf_counter() around a GPU call measure if there is no torch.cuda.synchronize()?
options: Twice the kernel time, since the launch and the run are both counted
The full kernel time, since perf_counter reads the GPU's own clock
Nothing at all, since perf_counter raises an error on GPU code
Mostly launch overhead, since Python returns as soon as the kernel is queued
questions.explanation: CUDA calls are asynchronous. Without a synchronize, the timer stops before the kernel finishes. CUDA events record timestamps on the GPU, which is why the procedure uses them.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 38.1 query the GPU instead of reading the spec sheet?
options: PyTorch refuses to run unless the specs have been queried first.
Spec sheets list Tensor Core speeds only, never memory sizes.
Clocks, power limits and SM counts vary between vendor versions.
The queried numbers include the CPU, which spec sheets leave out.
questions.explanation: The procedure's common mistake is assuming every card with the same name performs the same. An OEM-underclocked card is one example. Always query, never assume.

questions.prompt: For c = a*a + b, why does Procedure 38.3 count 3 arrays touched?
options: a is read twice, once for each factor of a*a, plus b once.
It reads a and b and writes c, so three arrays move through memory.
The multiply and the add each count as one array, plus the output array itself.
Every kernel counts three arrays by convention, whatever it does.
questions.explanation: Bytes moved counts every read and write: a in, b in, c out. a*a uses a's value twice but it is loaded once.

questions.prompt: c = a*a + b over 100 million fp32 elements touches 3 arrays and takes 1.28 ms. What is the achieved bandwidth in GB/s? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: Bytes = 10^8 × 3 × 4 = 1.2 × 10^9. Divided by 0.00128 s is 9.375 × 10^11 bytes/s, about 938 GB/s.

questions.prompt: A kernel reads two fp16 arrays of 50 million elements and writes one, taking 0.5 ms. What is its achieved bandwidth in GB/s?
questions.explanation: Bytes = 5 × 10^7 × 3 × 2 = 3 × 10^8. Divided by 0.0005 s is 6 × 10^11 bytes/s, which is 600 GB/s.

questions.prompt: The elementwise kernel reached about 55% of peak memory bandwidth and a tiny share of peak FLOPS. What does that mean for adding more arithmetic per element?
options: It would be nearly free. The kernel is memory-bound, so the cores are mostly waiting on bytes.
It can't be judged, since bandwidth and FLOPS can't be compared for one kernel.
It would halve speed, since the kernel is already at its FLOPS limit.
It would speed the kernel up, since more arithmetic improves cache reuse.
questions.explanation: The chapter calls this the book's first memory-bound workload: the bottleneck is moving bytes. Comparing against peak FLOPS is Procedure 38.3's common mistake, since the right ceiling here is bandwidth.

bookExercises.prompt: In one or two sentences, explain why a GPU is described as "throughput-optimised" and a CPU as "latency-optimised," using the SM/warp model from this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A GPU is throughput-optimised because it uses thousands of simple cores organized into SMs, each issuing one instruction per clock to a whole 32-thread warp, so it finishes millions of largely-uniform pieces of work fast in aggregate. A CPU is latency-optimised because its handful of complex cores (branch prediction, out-of-order execution, deep pipelines) are built to finish one thread of work as fast as possible, even when that thread is branchy or has unpredictable memory accesses.

bookExercises.prompt: Define warp divergence in your own words, and name the specific hardware feature that reduces its cost on Volta-onward GPUs.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Warp divergence is the performance cost that occurs when threads within the same 32-thread warp take different branches of a conditional, forcing the hardware to execute the branches serially (masking off inactive threads) in the classic model. The feature that reduces this cost on Volta-onward GPUs is **independent thread scheduling**, which lets diverged threads make progress more flexibly than the strict serial-branch model.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 38.3, compute the achieved bandwidth for a kernel that touches 4 arrays of fp32 data over 50 million elements in 0.9 ms. State whether the result looks memory-bound relative to this chapter's reference rig's ~1.7 TB/s estimated peak.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Using Listing 38.3's formula: `bytes_moved = 50_000_000 * 4 * 4 = 800,000,000` bytes = 0.8 GB. `achieved_bw = 0.8 / (0.9 / 1000) ≈ 889 GB/s`. Against this chapter's ~1.7 TB/s peak estimate, that is roughly 52% of peak, in the same range as the chapter's own 55% result, so this kernel also looks memory-bound rather than compute-bound, consistent with an elementwise-style operation.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 38.2's warm-up discipline, explain what would go wrong with the measured GPU time if the `warmup=5` loop were removed entirely, and why the effect would be worse on the very first run of a notebook than on the second.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Without the `warmup=5` loop, the timed run would include one-time CUDA context initialization and kernel JIT compilation costs, both of which are one-off costs unrelated to steady-state performance. The measured time would be dramatically inflated and would not reflect how fast the operation actually runs once "hot." This effect is worse on the very first run of a notebook specifically because CUDA context creation happens exactly once per process. Any call after that first one, even without an explicit warm-up loop, benefits from the context already existing, so a first-cell measurement without warm-up is the worst-case distortion.

bookExercises.prompt: This chapter measured a 75.4x speedup comparing one CPU core to the whole GPU. Using the SM count from Listing 38.1's output (170 SMs), sanity-check whether a naive "SM count times some per-core factor" estimate is a reasonable way to predict this kind of speedup, and explain what it leaves out.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A naive "170 SMs times some per-core speedup factor" estimate would wildly overshoot the measured 75.4x, because it ignores that the comparison is against a single CPU core (not 170 CPU-core-equivalents' worth of serial work), that the kernel measured is memory-bandwidth-bound (achieving only ~55% of peak bandwidth) rather than compute-bound, and that not every SM can be kept fully occupied for a workload this size relative to launch overhead. SM count sets an upper bound on parallel capacity, but actual speedup depends on occupancy, memory bandwidth, and how well the specific kernel is able to use all 170 SMs simultaneously, none of which a simple multiplication captures.

bookExercises.prompt: Design a workload (in one or two sentences, no code required) that you would expect to diverge expensively even on this chapter's modern, independent-thread-scheduling hardware, and explain what's different about it from Listing 38.5's kernels.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A workload with a data-dependent branch where one side does a slow, scattered global-memory lookup (e.g., a hash-table probe) and the other side does a cheap register-only computation would still diverge expensively on modern hardware. Independent thread scheduling lets threads make progress independently, but it does not eliminate the fact that a warp still has to wait for its slowest-diverged-path threads to finish before the warp can retire or reconverge. A scattered memory access is exactly the kind of high-latency, unpredictable-timing operation that widens that gap far more than the chapter's cheap-arithmetic branches did.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague argues that since the measured divergence overhead here was only 3.5%, warp divergence is no longer worth worrying about in kernel design. Write the two or three sentences you would say back, using this chapter's own caveats.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The 3.5% figure was measured on a workload where both branches did roughly equal, cheap, register-resident arithmetic. That is close to a best case for modern independent thread scheduling, not a general result. Divergence cost still scales with how unequal and how memory-latency-heavy the branches are, so a kernel with a genuinely expensive branch (a rare-but-slow code path, a scattered load) can still pay a real, large divergence penalty. The right habit is still to measure the actual kernel, not assume either "divergence is free" or "divergence costs 2x," since this chapter demonstrated both extremes are wrong as universal claims.

bookExercises.prompt: Skim the NVIDIA "Volta: Programmability and Performance" whitepaper's section on independent thread scheduling. Summarize, in a few sentences, the specific hardware mechanism that lets diverged threads make progress more flexibly than the pre-Volta model, and relate it to the measured 3.5% overhead in this chapter.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer expected. The Volta whitepaper describes giving each thread its own program counter and call stack, rather than one shared program counter per warp, so threads can diverge and reconverge more flexibly and the scheduler can choose to execute individual threads or subsets of a warp rather than forcing a strict "execute branch A for the whole warp, then branch B for the whole warp" ordering. That per-thread progress state is what lets a warp with cheap, roughly-balanced branches (as in this chapter's kernels) pay only a small scheduling overhead instead of the full serialized cost the classic model assumes. The 3.5% measured overhead reflects the residual cost of switching between per-thread execution states, not full serial re-execution of both branches.
